metadata.title: A Conservation Law Method in Optimization

extraction_notes.note: The six numbered equations of Section 1.1 (eqn:grad1 ... eqn:con2) sit in a numcases environment that latex_facts does not report; they are kept inside the example node ExP1 rather than emitted as separate equation nodes.
Experimental results are given as a table (Styblinski-Tang) and as nested enumerate lists of result matrices (Shekel); they stay inside the example ExP8 and the numerical claim ClP9.
Remark 3.4 asserts a result (saddle points are not detected) and defers its proof to Lee et al.; kept as remark with rigor semi_formal rather than retyped as claim.
Closing paragraph of Section 4.2 is a heuristic derivation ending in a decay-rate conclusion; emitted as one heuristic claim (alternative: remark), with Eq. (4.15) nested.
The sentence introducing the translation y_k = x_k - x* runs through both displayed schemes (4.1) and (4.2) with no sentence end, so the definition node spans both equations.

Newton's law in a conservative field, its phase-space form and the symplectic Euler scheme are classical but form the basis of the paper's method; marked external 'standard (uncited)' per Hard rule 3.
\include{notations} refers to a file not in the source (no macros appear affected); Remark 3.2 refers to lines 15 and 16 of Algorithm 1, which has only 15 printed lines.

Related-work discussion (except the cited Lee et al. result) and the conclusion's speculative proposals (fluid-dynamics and quantum-tunnelling search, O(log n) claim, KAM-theory question) were not made nodes.

nodes.name: Unconstrained optimization
nodes.statement:
Formally, the problem of unconstrained  optimization is stated in general terms as that of finding the minimum value that a function attains over Euclidean space, i.e.
$$
\mathop{\text{min}}_{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x).
$$
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $f(x)$ over $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: Gradient method
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& x_{k+1} = x_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k})\\
& \text{Any Initial Point}: \; x_{0}.
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Gradient descent iteration $x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k)$.
nodes.label: eqn:gradient

nodes.name: Polyak heavy ball method
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& x_{k+1} = x_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k}) + \gamma_{k} (x_{k} - x_{k-1})\\
& \text{Any Initial Point}: \; x_{0}.
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Momentum (heavy ball) iteration.
nodes.label: eqn:momentum

nodes.name: Condition number
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be the condition number, which is the ratio of the smallest eigenvalue and the largest eigenvalue of Hessian at local minima.
differentia: of the smallest eigenvalue and the largest eigenvalue of Hessian at local minima

nodes.name: Momentum method local convergence rate
nodes.statement: The momentum method speed up the local convergence rate from $1 - 2\kappa$ to $1 - 2\sqrt{\kappa}$.
conclusions: The momentum method speed up the local convergence rate from $1 - 2\kappa$ to $1 - 2\sqrt{\kappa}$.

nodes.name: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method
nodes.statement_short: Nesterov accelerated gradient iteration.
nodes.label: eqn:nesterov

nodes.name: Global convergence rates of Nesterov's scheme
nodes.statement: The scheme devised by Nesterov does not only own the property of the local convergence for strongly convex function, but also is the global convergence scheme, from $1 - 2\kappa$ to $1 - \sqrt{\kappa}$ for strongly convex function and from $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$ to $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)$ for non-strongly convex function.
conclusions: is the global convergence scheme, from $1 - 2\kappa$ to $1 - \sqrt{\kappa}$ for strongly convex function
from $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$ to $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)$ for non-strongly convex function
nodes.statement_short: Nesterov's method improves rates to $1-\sqrt{\kappa}$ (strongly convex) and $O(1/n^2)$ (convex), globally.

nodes.name: Gradient flow ODE
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x} = - \nabla f(x_{k})\\
& x(0)= x_{0},
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous-time limit of gradient descent.
nodes.label: eqn:gradient_system

nodes.name: Damped second-order ODE (heavy ball with friction)
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{x} + \gamma_{t} \dot{x} + \nabla f(x) = 0\\
& x(0)= x_{0}, \;\dot{x}(0) =0,
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.origin_citation: Polyak 1964; Su, Boyd & Candes 2014; Wibisono et al. 2016
nodes.statement_short: Continuous-time limit of momentum and Nesterov methods with friction $\gamma_t$.
nodes.label: eqn:2nd_system

nodes.name: Key observation: velocity is observable and controllable
nodes.statement: The key observation in this paper is that we find the kinetic energy, or the velocity, is observable and controllable variable in the optimization process. In other words, we can compare the velocities in every step to look for local minimum in the computational process or re-set them to zero to arrive to artificially dissipate energy.
nodes.statement_short: Kinetic energy (velocity) can be monitored and reset during optimization to find local minima or dissipate energy.

nodes.name: Newton's second law in a conservative force field
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& \ddot{x} = - \nabla f(x) \\
&  x(0)= x_{0}, \;\dot{x}(0) =0. 
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Frictionless motion $\ddot x=-\nabla f(x)$ from rest.
nodes.label: eqn:conservation

nodes.name: Phase space
nodes.statement: The concept of phase space, developed in the late 19th century, usually consists of all possible values of position and momentum variables.
differentia: consists of all possible values of position and momentum variables

nodes.name: Conservation-law ODE in phase space
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
& \dot{x} = v \\
& \dot{v} = -\nabla f(x) \\
&  x(0)= x_{0}, \;v(0) =0 .
\end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: First-order (position, velocity) form of the frictionless dynamics.
nodes.label: eqn:conphase

nodes.name: Two velocity-based strategies
nodes.statement_short: Strategy 1: reset velocity when its norm stops increasing (local minima); strategy 2: start with large velocity and record kinetic-energy maxima to locate local minima.

nodes.name: Analytical demonstration on $f(x)=\frac{1}{200}x^2$
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form solutions of gradient flow, damped ODE and frictionless ODE for a 1-D ill-conditioned quadratic.

nodes.name: Iteration-count estimate $n\sim\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{L/\mu}$
nodes.statement:
From the analytical solution for local convex quadratic function with maximum eigenvalue $L$ and minimum eigenvalue $\mu$, in general, the step size by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}$ for momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method, hence the simple estimate for iterative times is approximately 
$$
n \sim \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}.
$$ 
hence, the iterative times $n$ is proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of minimal eigenvalue $\sqrt{\mu}$, which is essentially different from the convergence rate of the gradient method and momentum method.
assumptions: local convex quadratic function with maximum eigenvalue $L$ and minimum eigenvalue $\mu$
nodes.statement_short: With step $1/\sqrt{L}$, stopping at maximal velocity needs about $\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{L/\mu}$ iterations.

nodes.name: Gradient descent converges to local minima almost everywhere
nodes.statement: From the stability theorem of ODE, the gradient method always converges to local minima in the sense of almost everywhere is proposed in~\citep{lee2016gradient}.
conclusions: the gradient method always converges to local minima in the sense of almost everywhere

nodes.name: Symplectic Euler scheme
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
         & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + h v_{k+1} \\
         & v_{k+1} = v_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k})
        \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: First-order symplectic Euler discretization of the Hamiltonian system.
nodes.label: eqn:symplectic_euler

nodes.name: Remark 3.1 (Störmer-Verlet alternative)
nodes.statement:
In all the algorithms below, the symplectic Euler scheme can be taken place by the St\"{o}rmer-Verlet scheme, i.e.  
\begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned}
        & v_{k+1/2} = v_{k} - \frac{h}{2}\nabla f(x_{k}) \\
        & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + h v_{k + 1/2} \\
        & v_{k+1} = v_{k + 1/2} - \frac{h}{2} \nabla f(x_{k+1})
        \end{aligned}\right. 
\end{equation}
which works perfectly better than the symplectic scheme even if doubling step size and keep the left-right symmetry of the Hamiltonian system. The St\"{o}rmer-Verlet scheme is the natural discretization for 2nd-order ODE
\begin{equation} x_{k+1} - 2x_{k} + x_{k-1} = -h^{2}\nabla f(x_{k})
\end{equation}
which is named as leap-frog scheme in PDEs. We remark that the discrete scheme~(\ref{eqn:discrete}) is different from the finite difference approximation by the forward Euler method to analyze the stability of 2nd ODE in~\citep{su2014differential}, since the momentum term is biased.
nodes.statement_short: The symplectic Euler step can be replaced by the Störmer-Verlet (leap-frog) scheme, which is better and differs from forward-Euler discretizations.

nodes.name: Störmer-Verlet scheme
nodes.statement:
\left\{\begin{aligned}
        & v_{k+1/2} = v_{k} - \frac{h}{2}\nabla f(x_{k}) \\
        & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + h v_{k + 1/2} \\
        & v_{k+1} = v_{k + 1/2} - \frac{h}{2} \nabla f(x_{k+1})
        \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Second-order Störmer-Verlet (half-step velocity) scheme.
nodes.label: eqn:symplectic_vertex

nodes.name: Artificially Dissipating Energy Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Symplectic Euler simulation of frictionless motion, resetting the velocity to zero whenever its norm stops increasing.
nodes.label: alg:local

nodes.name: Remark 3.2 (implementation)
nodes.statement: In the actual algorithm~\ref{alg:local}, the codes in line $15$ and $16$ are not need in the while loop in order to  speed up the computation.

nodes.name: Ill-conditioned 2-D quadratic
nodes.statement:
Here, we use a simple convex quadratic function with ill-conditioned eigenvalue for illustration as below,
\begin{equation} f(x_1, x_{2}) = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}^{2} + \alpha x_{2}^{2}\right),
\end{equation}
of which the maximum eigenvalue is $L=1$ and the minimum eigenvalue is $\mu = \alpha$.  Hence the scale of the step size for~(\ref{eqn:artifical1}) is 
$$
\frac{1}{L} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}} = 1.
$$
In figure~\ref{fig:common}, we demonstrate the convergence rate of gradient method, momentum method, Nesterov accelerated gradient method and artifically dissipating energy  method with the common step size $h = 0.1$ and $h = 0.5$, where the optimal friction parameter for momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method $\gamma = \frac{1-\sqrt{\alpha}}{1+\sqrt{\alpha}}$ with $\alpha = 10^{-5}$.  A further result for comparison with the optimal step size in gradient method $h = \frac{2}{1+\alpha}$, the momentum method $h = \frac{4}{(1+\sqrt{\alpha})^{2}}$, and Nesterov accelerated gradient method with $h=1$ and the artifically disspating energy  method with $h=0.5$ shown in figure~\ref{fig:diff}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare gradient, momentum, Nesterov and artificially dissipating energy methods on $\frac12(x_1^2+\alpha x_2^2)$.

nodes.name: Faster convergence of the artificially dissipating energy method
nodes.statement: A clear fact in figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} shows that the gradient correction decrease the oscillation to comparing with momentum method. A more clear observation is that artificially dissipating method owns the same property with the other three method by the law of nature, that is, if the trajectory come into the local minima in one dimension will not leave it very far. However, from figure~\ref{fig:common} and figure~\ref{fig:diff}, the more rapid convergence rate from artificially dissipating energy method has been shown.
conclusions: the more rapid convergence rate from artificially dissipating energy method has been shown
nodes.statement_short: On the quadratic test, the artificially dissipating energy method converges faster than the other three methods.

nodes.name: Energy Conservation Algorithm
nodes.section: 3.2 Energy Conservation Algorithm For Detecting Local Minima
nodes.statement_short: Simulate frictionless motion with initial velocity and record positions where the speed has a local maximum (candidate local minima).
nodes.label: alg:global

nodes.name: Remark 3.3
nodes.statement: In the algorithm~\ref{alg:global}, we can set $v_{0} > 0$ such that the total energy large enough to climb up some high peak. Same as the algorithm~\ref{alg:local}, the function value $f(x)$ is not need in the while loop in order to  speed up the computation.
nodes.section: 3.2 Energy Conservation Algorithm For Detecting Local Minima

nodes.name: 1-D piecewise cosine non-convex function
nodes.statement:
Here, we use the non-convex function for illustration as below,
\begin{equation} f(x) = \left\{\begin{aligned}
                 & 2\cos(x),     && x \in [0,2\pi]      \\
                 & \cos(x) + 1, && x \in [2\pi, 4\pi]  \\
                 & 3\cos(x) -1, && x \in [4\pi, 6\pi]  
                 \end{aligned}\right.
\end{equation}
which is the 2nd-order smooth function but not 3rd-order smooth. The maximum eigenvalue can be calculated as below
$$
\max\limits_{x\in [0,6\pi]} |f''(x)| = 3.
$$
then, the step length is set $h \sim \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}}$. We illustrate that the algorithm~\ref{alg:global} simulate the trajectory and find the local minima in figure~\ref{fig:noncon1}.
nodes.statement_short: Energy conservation algorithm locates local minima of a piecewise cosine on $[0,6\pi]$.

nodes.name: Piecewise cosine test function
nodes.statement:
f(x) = \left\{\begin{aligned}
                 & 2\cos(x),     && x \in [0,2\pi]      \\
                 & \cos(x) + 1, && x \in [2\pi, 4\pi]  \\
                 & 3\cos(x) -1, && x \in [4\pi, 6\pi]  
                 \end{aligned}\right.
nodes.label: eqn:noncon1

nodes.name: 2-D sinusoidal potential
nodes.statement:
Another 2D potential function is shown as below,
\begin{equation} f(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{2} \left[\left(x_1 - 4\right)^{2} + \left(x_2 - 4\right)^{2} + 8\sin(x_1 + 2x_2)\right].
\end{equation}
which is the  smooth function with domain in $(x_{1},x_{2}) \in [0,8]\times [0,8]$. The maximum eigenvalue can be calculated as below
$$
\max\limits_{x\in [0,6\pi]} |\lambda(f''(x))| \geq 16.
$$
then, the step length is set $h \sim \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}}$. We illustrate that the algorithm~\ref{alg:global} simulate the trajectory and find the local minima in figure~\ref{fig:noncon2}.
nodes.statement_short: Energy conservation algorithm locates local minima of a 2-D quadratic-plus-sine potential.

nodes.name: 2-D sinusoidal potential
nodes.statement: f(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{2} \left[\left(x_1 - 4\right)^{2} + \left(x_2 - 4\right)^{2} + 8\sin(x_1 + 2x_2)\right].
nodes.label: eqn:noncon2

nodes.name: Remark 3.4 (saddle points not detected)
nodes.statement: We point out that for the energy conservation algorithm for detecting local minima along the trajectory cannot detect saddle point in the sense of almost everywhere, since the saddle point in original function $f(x)$ is also a saddle point for the energy function $H(x,v) = \frac{1}{2}\|v\|^{2} + f(x)$. The proof process is fully the same in~\citep{lee2016gradient}.
nodes.statement_short: The energy conservation algorithm almost surely does not detect saddle points, as saddles of $f$ are saddles of $H(x,v)$.

nodes.name: Combined Algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Detect candidate local minima with the energy conservation algorithm, refine each with the artificially dissipating energy algorithm, and take the best.
nodes.label: alg:combined

nodes.name: Remark 3.5 (no global guarantee)
nodes.statement: We remark that the combined algorithm (algorithm~\ref{alg:combined}) cannot guarantee to find global minima if the initial position is not ergodic. The tracking local minima is dependent on the trajectory. However, the time of computation and precision based on the proposed algorithm is far better than the large sampled gradient method. Our proposed algorithm first makes the global minima found become possible.
nodes.statement_short: The combined algorithm cannot guarantee global minima without ergodic initialization but is far cheaper than sampled gradient descent.

nodes.name: Locally linearized symplectic Euler scheme
nodes.section: 4 An Asymptotic Analysis for The Phenomena of Local High-Speed Convergence
nodes.statement_short: Linearization of the translated scheme at the local minimum using the Hessian.
nodes.label: eqn:equiv_linear

nodes.name: Remark 4.1 (validity of linearization)
nodes.statement: The local linearized analysis is based on the stability theorem in finite dimension, the invariant stable manifold theorem and Hartman-Grobman linearized map theorem~\citep{hartman1982ordinary}. The thought is firstly used in~\citep{polyak1964some} to estimate the local convergence of momentum method. And in the paper~\citep{lee2016gradient}, the thought is used to exclude the possiblity to converegnce to saddle point. However, the two theorems above belong to the qualitative theorem of ODE. Hence, the linearized scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}) is only an approximate estimate for the original scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_sym}) locally.
nodes.section: 4 An Asymptotic Analysis for The Phenomena of Local High-Speed Convergence
nodes.statement_short: Linearization is justified by stable-manifold and Hartman-Grobman theorems, but only qualitatively, so it is an approximation.

nodes.name: Hessian matrix $A$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the positive-semidefinite and symmetric matrix to represent $\nabla^{2}f(x^{\star})$ in~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}).

nodes.label: lem:equiv

M

nodes.name: Block-diagonalization of $M$
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
assumptions: where $\omega_{i}^{2}$ is the eigenvalue of the matrix $A$.
conclusions: there exists the orthogonal transformation $U_{2n\times 2n}$ such that the matrix $M$ is similar as below
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is orthogonally similar to a block-diagonal matrix of $2\times2$ blocks $T_i$ determined by the eigenvalues $\omega_i^2$ of $A$.
nodes.label: lem:symmetric

nodes.name: Block-diagonal form
nodes.statement: U^{T}MU = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix}
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: $2\times 2$ block $T_i$
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
nodes.label: eqn:2by2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be the diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ as below
$$
\Lambda =\begin{pmatrix} \omega^{2}_{1} & & & \\ &\omega^{2}_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & \omega^{2}_{n} \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Since $A$ is positive definite and symmetric, there exists orthogonal matrix $U_{1}$ such that 
$$
U_{1}^{T}AU_{1} =  \Lambda.
$$
Let $\Pi$ be the permuation matrix satisfying 
$$
\Pi_{i,j} = \left\{
      \begin{aligned}
       &1, && j\;\text{odd},\;  i=\frac{j+1}{2} \\
       &1, && j\;\text{even},\; i=n+\frac{j}{2} \\
       &0, && \text{otherwise}
      \end{aligned}
      \right.   
$$
where $i$ is the row index and $j$ is the column index. Then, let $U = \mathbf{diag}(U_{1},U_{1})\Pi$, we have by conjugation
$$
\begin{aligned}
U^{T}MU & =\Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1}^{T} & \\ & U_{1}^{T}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}I-h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1} & \\ & U_{1}\end{pmatrix}\Pi \\
        & = \Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} I-h^2\Lambda & hI \\ -h\Lambda & I \end{pmatrix} \Pi\\
        & = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix}  
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize $A$ orthogonally, then permute coordinates to interleave position and velocity, giving the $2\times2$ blocks.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues of $T_i$ on the unit circle

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement:
For $i = 1, \ldots, n$, we have
$$
\left|\lambda I - T_{i}\right| = 0\Leftrightarrow \lambda_{1,2} = 1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2} \pm h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}.
$$

nodes.statement_short: Solve the characteristic equation of $T_i$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Sine identities
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
nodes.label: eqn:coorpro

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement:
With Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function, we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(\theta_{i} + \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}+ \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\
                            & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} + \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = \sin\phi_{i}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $0< h\omega_{i} < 2$, we have $\theta_{i}, \phi_{i} \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we can obtain that 
$$
\theta_{i} + \phi_{i} = \pi - \phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i}
$$
and with the coordinate transfornation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have
$$
\sin\theta_{i} = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \sin(2\phi_{i}) = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i}.
$$
Next, we use Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function furthermore, 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(\theta_{i} - \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}- \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\
                            & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} - \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = \left(h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}-1\right)\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$
and with $\theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i}$, we have
$$
\sin(3\phi_{i}) = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i}
$$
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

Comparing~(\ref{eqn:sol}) and~(\ref{eqn:equivtran}), we can obtain that 
$$

nodes.name: Remark 4.8 (step size and ODE behaviour)
nodes.statement: Here, the behavior is similar as the thought in~\citep{lee2016gradient}. The step size $0<hL<2$ make sure the global convergence of gradient method. And the step size $0<hL<1$ make the uniqueness of the trajectory along the gradient method, the thought of which is equivalent of the existencen and uniqueness of the solution for ODE. Actually, the step size $0<hL<1$ owns the property with the solution of ODE, the continous-limit version. A global existence of the solution for gradient system is proved in~\citep{perko2013differential}.
nodes.statement_short: Relates step-size ranges $0<hL<2$ and $0<hL<1$ to convergence and trajectory uniqueness, as in Lee et al.

nodes.name: Velocity reset occurs near a quarter period
nodes.statement:
For every ill-conditioned eigen-direction, with every initial condition $(y_{0},0)^{T}$, if the algorithm~\ref{alg:local} is implemented at $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$, then there exist an eigenvalue $\omega_{i}^{2}$ such that 
$$k\omega_{i} h \geq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$
assumptions: For every ill-conditioned eigen-direction, with every initial condition $(y_{0},0)^{T}$
if the algorithm~\ref{alg:local} is implemented at $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$
conclusions: there exist an eigenvalue $\omega_{i}^{2}$ such that $$k\omega_{i} h \geq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: When Algorithm 1 first resets the velocity, some eigen-direction has completed a quarter period $k\omega_i h\ge\pi/2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.9
nodes.statement:
When $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$, then $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$. While for the $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$, we can write in the analytical form, 
$$
\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_{i}^{2}(U_{1}y_{0})_{i}^{2}\sin^{2}(kh\omega_{i})}
$$
if there is no $k\omega_{i} h < \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$ increase with $k$ increasing.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\|U_1^Tv\|$ in closed form; if no direction reached $\pi/2$ the norm would still be increasing.

nodes.name: Rapid decay near the quarter period
nodes.statement:
For some $i$ such that $k\omega_{i}h$ approximating $\frac{\pi}{2}$, we have
\begin{equation} \begin{aligned}
\frac{\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k+1,i}\right|}{\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i}\right|} & = \frac{\cos\left((k+1)h\omega_{i}\right)}{\cos\left(kh\omega_{i}\right)} \\
                                                                                                        & = e^{\ln\cos\left((k+1)h\omega_{i}\right) - \ln \cos\left(kh\omega_{i}\right) } \\
                                                                                                        & = e^{-\tan(\xi) h\omega_{i}}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\xi \in \left(kh\omega_{i}, (k+1)h\omega_{i}\right)$. Hence, with $\xi$ approximating $\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i}\right|$ approximatie $0$ with the linear convergence, but the coefficient will also decay with the rate $e^{-\tan(\xi) h\omega_{i}}$ with $\xi \rightarrow \frac{\pi}{2}$. With the Laurent expansion for $\tan \xi$ at $\frac{\pi}{2}$, i.e.,
$$
\tan \xi = -\frac{1}{\xi - \frac{\pi}{2}} +\frac{1}{3} \left(\xi - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{45} \left(\xi - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{3} + \mathcal{O}\left(\left(\xi - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{5}\right)
$$  
the coefficient has the approximating formula
$$ 
e^{-\tan(\xi) h\omega_{i}} \approx e^{ \frac{h\omega_{i}}{\xi - \frac{\pi}{2}}} \leq \left(\frac{\pi}{2} -\xi \right)^{n}.
$$
where $n$ is an arbitrary large real number in $\mathbb{R}^{+}$ for $\xi \rightarrow \frac{\pi}{2}$.
conclusions: $\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i}\right|$ approximatie $0$ with the linear convergence, but the coefficient will also decay with the rate $e^{-\tan(\xi) h\omega_{i}}$ with $\xi \rightarrow \frac{\pi}{2}$
nodes.statement_short: Near $kh\omega_i\approx\pi/2$ the contraction factor $e^{-\tan(\xi)h\omega_i}$ tends to zero, explaining the local high-speed convergence.

nodes.name: Strongly convex quadratic experiments
nodes.statement:
Here, we investigate the artificially dissipating energy algorithm (algorithm~\ref{alg:local}) for the strongly convex function for comparison with gradient method, momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method (strongly convex case) by the quadratic function as below. 
\begin{equation} f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^{T} Ax + b^{T}x
\end{equation}
where $A$ is symmetric and positive-definite matrix.  The two cases are shown as below:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(\alph*)}]
\item The generative matrix $A$ is $500\times 500$ random positive definite matrix with eigenvalue from $1e-6$ to $1$ with one defined eigenvalue $1e-6$. The generative vector $b$ follows  i.i.d. Gaussian distribution with mean $0$ and variance $1$.  
\item The generative matrix $A$ is the notorious example in Nesterov's book~\citep{nesterov2013introductory}, i.e.,
         $$
         A = \begin{pmatrix}
                2 & -1 &   &  &&\\
                -1 &2  &-1&  &&\\
                    &-1 & 2 &\ddots  &&\\
                    &     &\ddots  &\ddots &\ddots &            \\
                    &     &  &\ddots  &\ddots       &-1   \\
                    &      &          &   & -1   &2  
               \end{pmatrix}
         $$
         the eigenvalues of the matrix are
         $$
         \lambda_{k} = 2 - 2\cos\left(\frac{k\pi}{n+1}\right) = 4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{k\pi}{2(n+1)}\right)
         $$ 
         and $n$ is the dimension of the matrix $A$. The eigenvector can be solved by the second Chebyshev's polynomial. We implement $\dim(A) = 1000$   
         and $b$ is zero vector.  Hence, the smallest eigenvalue is approximating
         $$
         \lambda_{1} = 4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\right) \approx \frac{\pi^{2}}{1001^{2}} \approx 10^{-5}
         $$
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm 1 vs gradient, momentum and Nesterov on a random 500-dim ill-conditioned quadratic and Nesterov's tridiagonal example.

$$

nodes.statement:
Since $A$ is positive definite and symmetric, there exists orthogonal matrix $U_{1}$ such that 
$$
U_{1}^{T}AU_{1} =  \Lambda.
$$

nodes.name: Sum identity
nodes.statement:
With Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function, we have 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(\theta_{i} + \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}+ \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\
                            & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} + \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\
                            & = \sin\phi_{i}.
\end{aligned}
$$
nodes.statement_short: Show $\sin(\theta_i+\phi_i)=\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Angle relation
nodes.statement:
Since $0< h\omega_{i} < 2$, we have $\theta_{i}, \phi_{i} \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we can obtain that 
$$
\theta_{i} + \phi_{i} = \pi - \phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i}
$$
and with the coordinate transfornation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have
$$
\sin\theta_{i} = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \sin(2\phi_{i}) = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i}.
$$
nodes.statement_short: Deduce $\theta_i=\pi-2\phi_i$ and $\sin 2\phi_i=h\omega_i\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
